How does a brainless colony find the shortest path through a maze without a map or a leader? The answer lies in a phenomenon called Stigmergy—a form of decentralized coordination where individuals interact through chemical modifications to their environment.
This simulation brings Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) to life, modeling the precise feedback loops that govern swarm intelligence. Each autonomous agent manages two distinct data streams: a Home Trail and a Food Trail. As ants navigate between their nest and a resource, they deposit volatile pheromones. Because ants on a shorter path complete their round-trips faster, they reinforce their route with more pheromone per unit of time compared to those on longer detours. This creates a Positive Feedback Loop, rapidly recruiting the rest of the colony to the most efficient trajectory.
The underlying mechanics are governed by a discrete approximation of the Diffusion-Evaporation Equation: ∂τ/∂t = Δτ + D∇²τ - ρτ. This equation balances three critical factors: the recruitment of new trail (Δτ), the spatial spread of information via diffusion (D), and the pruning of weak or obsolete data through exponential decay (ρ). creator: simulateitnow
title: Shepherd dog flock simulation — pressure-field + boids rules
summary: @simulateitnow explains a flock-herding simulation combining a pressure-field force F=(1-d/R)^1.2 with classic boids (cohesion/alignment/separation). Great reference for swarm/multi-agent simulation math.
caption:
A single shepherd dog can control an entire flock of sheep without ever touching them. The secret is spatial pressure — the exploitation of every prey animal's flight zone.
When a predator (or herding dog) enters the flight zone — the minimum distance at which an animal perceives a threat — the animal moves away. The dog does not chase individual sheep. Instead, it positions itself behind the flock relative to the target destination. This creates a directional pressure wave that pushes the entire group forward.
The pressure force follows an inverse-distance relationship: F = (1 − d/R)^1.2, where R is the pressure radius. Sheep closer to the dog flee harder. Sheep at the edge barely react. This gradient is what gives the dog fine control over the flock's direction.
The sheep themselves follow boids rules — three local interaction forces that produce emergent flocking:
Cohesion: steer toward the average position of nearby neighbors
Alignment: match heading with neighbors
Separation: avoid crowding
When the dog's pressure disrupts this equilibrium, the flock compresses, redirects, and flows toward the pen. Stubborn sheep dampen their flee response, requiring the dog to close distance
transcript: A single dog controls 60 sheep without any commands. It uses nothing but spatial pressure. The pressure radius defines the zone. Everything inside that circle moves away from the dog. A wider radius means the dog controls more sheep at once. Total flock control. Shrink the radius and the dog must chase harder. The sheep scatter in every direction. Cohesion is the glue holding the flock together. It determines how tightly they pack. High cohesion and the flock moves as a single dense ball. One unit easy to herd. Low cohesion and individuals break away. Total chaos for the dog. Stubborn sheep resist the dog's pressure. They refuse to flee as easily. Maximum stubbornness and sheep plant their feet. They barely move even when pressured. Zero stubbornness and they are completely docile. The dog herds them effortlessly. Now a faster dog. Watch what happens when we increase the speed. The dog covers the entire field. No sheep escapes its reach. Real shepherd dogs use these exact pressure mechanics every day. This is how it works. Explore at simulatednow.com

1. In 1924, researcher Elton Mayo conducted an experiment that many later tried to bury.

He told workers they were being «observed for productivity.» And it was true—they were constantly monitored. Yet within weeks, something shifted: more focus, higher output, greater initiative. A simple observation changed real behavior—as if the brain had received a silent command.

2. Years later, other researchers repeated the study—this time with self-observation.

One group was told they possessed an «internal monitoring ability.» The tasks were identical, but those who observed their own thoughts produced responses that were 94% more accurate.

The scientists were clear: «We didn’t increase ability. We changed the way they observed themselves.»

A simple reversal strategy on crypto:
If the price goes up, go short and If the price goes down, go long.

Dollar-neutral means total longs equals total shorts.
Positions are scaled so total absolute exposure stays equals 1, keeping risk consistent.

Without considering any transaction costs, the results seem good. With transaction costs, however, the returns vanish quickly.

But I found this is still a good start when learning before starting to explore other signals and strategies.

npm run deploy

When you’re about to spawn a sub-agent:
• it understands what you want to do
• checks if the action is directly executable
• and if AI isn’t needed…

👉 it suggests running it directly in the terminal

• it opens the terminal
• injects the command
• runs it instantly

we run npm run deploy
and instead of starting the agent → PromptOps suggests the terminal.
Simple, but it changes everything:
• fewer wasted tokens
• faster execution
• AI used only when it actually matters

At the end of the day:
AI should think, not execute what’s already ready.
